newsitem.title: USA: Fla tobacco cases will not be settled with Liggett.
newsitem.headline: Fla tobacco cases will not be settled with Liggett.

text.p: Documents from the Liggett settlement could affect two landmark Florida class-action lawsuits against the major tobacco firms which are not included in the Ligget settlement, plaintiffs lawyers said on Friday.

Stanley Rosenblatt, the Miami attorney who launched the two cases, known as Broin vs. Philip Morris and Engle vs. R.J. Reynolds, said his firm had not discussed a settlement with Liggett and would not settle with Liggett.
"Our people will not be a part of any Liggett settlement," he said after a pre-trial hearing in the Engle case.
Rosenblatt said he was uncertain what part the documents to be released by Liggett as part of a national settlement would play in the Engle and Broin lawsuits.

But he said if press reports were accurate that the documents contained Liggett lawyers' notes demonstrating "how companies including Liggett tried to withhold the truth," the documents would be useful.
"If that's written down, that's very good evidence," he said.

The Engle lawsuit, brought on behalf of physician Howard Engle and others, claims that tobacco companies failed to protect consumers from the dangers of smoking and that thousands of those consumers became addicted to cigarettes and suffered tobacco-related illnesses. It was scheduled to go to trial September 8.
In the Broin case, set for trial on June 2, flight attendants claim they were sickened by second-hand smoke on the job.

Liggett Group Inc. on Thursday settled lawsuits filed by attorneys general in 22 states. Officials said as part of the settlement, Liggett admitted that tobacco was addictive, caused cancer and that tobacco firms marketed to minors.
Liggett agreed to turn over documents to state judges that could prove crucial in lawsuits against other tobacco firms.

Dade County Judge Alan Postman said during Friday's pre-trial hearing that he wanted to see the Liggett documents as soon as possible and would enter an order next week for Liggett to produce them unless a higher court had ordered them kept secret.
"I think those documents should be delivered to me for review in camera," Postman told lawyers. "Unless I see an order, I'm going to assume there isn't one in place."
Tobacco company lawyers objected to Postman ordering the documents be turned over, saying they might have nothing to do with the Engle lawsuit.
"I have the feeling they have everything to do with it," Postman said.
Robert Heim, an attorney for Philip Morris, downplayed the impact of the settlement and usefulness of the Liggett papers.
"I think its significance in the long run is not anywhere near what the politicians want to make of it," Heim said. "It's still going to come down to how jurors react."

Defendants in the Engle suit include Philip Morris Cos Inc, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc, Lorillard Tobacco Co, a unit of Loews Corp and Liggett Group Inc, a unit of Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd.
